articles.title: California’s billionaire tax faces a precarious road from rich opposition
articles.summary: Tech billionaires have raised more than $300m to oppose the billionaire tax proposal.
articles.body:
San Francisco, United States – University of California at Berkeley economics professor Brian Galle recently found a flyer in his mailbox about the proposed billionaire tax he helped write. But as he read it, Galle found things he hadn’t written, including that the tax can be on anyone and even on their retirement savings.

Californians have been getting such flyers and watching similar ads as they prepare to vote in the November 3 election on whether to impose the one-time tax of 5 percent on the assets of the state’s billionaires.

Spending by the billionaires to oppose the tax has made this the most expensive ballot measure ever and among the most expensive campaigns of this midterm, says David McCuan, professor of political science at Sonoma State University, who tracks state and local elections.

California’s celebrated tech billionaires, including Google co-founder Sergey Brin, Doordash founder Tony Xu, Stripe co-founder Patrick Collison, Ripple co-executive chairman Chris Larsen and venture capitalists John Doerr, Michael Moritz and Vinod Khosla, are among those who have donated more than $300m to block the additional tax on their assets.

While Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg has not donated money to oppose the tax, Meta’s SEC filings revealed that he told the company’s board, which includes Xu and Collison, that he would buy a home outside California to avoid paying the tax. This could have affected Meta stock prices and the board created a new class of shares that Zuckerberg could use to pay the tax.

The billionaire fundraising has far outstripped that of the supporters, who only raised $32m. This has led to the ubiquitous ad campaign as well as outreach to voters.

“I feel like I am in an Alice in Wonderland alternate reality,” said Ashley Craig, a volunteer for Patriotic Millionaires, a group that supports the tax.

Craig has spent months door knocking and making calls to voters to campaign for the tax and often hears misinformation about it.

“They often tell me it has secret provisions allowing everyone to be taxed, which is not entirely true,” she said.

Any change in the tax would require a two-thirds majority in the assembly and would need to stay true to the spirit of the tax. But the prevalence of the ads has meant that voters often tell Craig the tax would soon include her – and them.

“The irony is that Prop 40 [the billionaire tax proposal] is meant to make democracy more equal, but the billionaires are using their money to avoid that,” says Galle, the proposal’s coauthor.

The US Supreme Court’s judgement in the Citizens United v FEC case gave companies and special groups the freedom to spend freely in elections, he said.

“This has led to this situation where Sergey Brin has a lot more of a political voice,” says Francesco Trebbi, the BT Rocca professor of Business and Public Policy at the University of California at Berkeley’s Haas School of Business. “It’s Sergey Brin v millions of Californians. This leads people to lose trust in the system ” .

Apart from the ad buys, Craig says she has also felt alone in the campaign arena. While the state Democratic party has endorsed the tax proposal, Craig says she hasn’t had ground support from the party. “We don’t have resources like social media, door knocking, phone banking and I would place the blame at the feet of the Democratic party.”

Sonoma State’s McCuan attributes this to the Democratic party’s internal rift between the progressives and moderates, with the former in favour of such a policy and the latter resisting it.

“This is a broader proxy test between the party’s progressives and moderates. If this works, progressive candidates could try such ideas in the 2028 presidential elections,” McCuan says, which the billionaires and moderates want to avert.

So while the party has endorsed the measure, California Governor Gavin Newsom has opposed it, as has Xavier Becerra, the Democratic candidate for governor in the election and Katie Porter, a former congresswoman who also ran for governor.

Newsom, who is eyeing a 2028 presidential run, has opposed the tax, saying it is “poorly written. It would harm the state if its billionaires, who have an estimated wealth of 2.3 trillion according to the measure’s authors, move, as Zuckerberg has planned,” Newsom has said.

The tax’s opponents have also backed a ballot measure that prohibits any new state taxes based on personal property or imposed retroactively. Another asks state auditors to review any proposed tax measures for their financial impact before they are voted on. If these pass and get more votes than the billionaire tax, they could negate the billionaire tax, even if it is passed.

Only a third of citizen initiatives pass

The strong campaign opposing the billionaire tax may have impacted support for it. Voters support the tax by a small margin, but also the two measures that oppose it, according to a recent poll by the Public Policy Institute of California (PPIC).

“Only about a third of such citizen initiatives pass. So the burden is on the yes side,” says Mark Baldassare, statewide survey director and Miller chair in public policy at PPIC. “Support can decline if people don’t feel completely sure.”

But Suzane Jiminez, chief of staff at the SEIU health workers union, which has sponsored the billionaire tax measure, said, “We are feeling confident that we will have the votes. When voters see that billionaires are funding the ads, they see through them.”

Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Congressman Ro Khanna of California rallied across the state to drum up support for the measure. Jiminez said that in the last few weeks, 3,000 volunteers have spread out to knock on doors and distributed flyers explaining the tax across the state. “The democratic figureheads do not represent the rank and file on this. They are supporting us,” Jiminez said.

It is unclear whether this will be enough, as the shortfall in funding means support for the measure remains precarious. Baldassare said he plans to do his poll again as voters read and receive the state’s voter guides explaining the ballot measures and make up their minds.

Sonoma University’s McCuan said that just the historic amount of money being spent on defeating the measure is a win in itself for the tax backers.

“Progressives can win by losing. They can say moderates sank us, use it as a morality play. They will attack big tech – as a bad bogeyman of US politics.”

articles.title: Mumbai-Bengaluru, Delhi-Varanasi Vande Bharat Sleeper trains: Routes, timings, fares and key details
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Indian Railways is set to expand its premium overnight train network with two new Vande Bharat Sleeper services connecting Mumbai and
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Indian Railways is set to expand its premium overnight train network with two new Vande Bharat Sleeper services connecting Mumbai and Bengaluru, and Varanasi and New Delhi. The Bengaluru-Mumbai service is scheduled to be inaugurated on October 31, followed by the Varanasi-New Delhi service on November 1.The two services are expected to provide faster overnight connectivity for business travellers, working professionals, students, pilgrims and tourists. The Mumbai-Bengaluru train is expected to cover the nearly 1,000km journey in 15 hours and 45 minutes, while the Varanasi-New Delhi service will run overnight via Prayagraj and Kanpur.The new routes will add to the existing Vande Bharat Sleeper network, which currently operates between Howrah and Kamakhya.Mumbai-Bengaluru Vande Bharat SleeperRoute and stopsThe proposed Mumbai-Bengaluru Vande Bharat Sleeper will connect Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus (CSMT) in Mumbai with Sir M Visvesvaraya Terminal (SMVT) in Bengaluru. The route will pass through Kalyan, Pune, Solapur, Kalaburagi, Raichur, Guntakal and Anantapur.The service will connect two major economic centres in Maharashtra and Karnataka, offering another travel option for people commuting between the cities for work, business and tourism.The train has completed its trial run at speeds of up to 160kmph. Two Vande Bharat Sleeper trainsets have been proposed for the route. The service is expected to operate six days a week, although the schedule and other operational details remain tentative and are subject to official confirmation.Timings and travel timeAccording to the tentative schedule, the Mumbai-Bengaluru Vande Bharat Sleeper will depart from CSMT at 8.10pm and reach SMVT Bengaluru at 11.55am the following day.In the return direction, the train is expected to leave Bengaluru at 7.50pm and arrive at CSMT at 11.55am the next day.The proposed service will cover the journey in 15 hours and 45 minutes, reducing travel time by around six hours and 20 minutes compared with the existing Udyan Express.Delhi-Varanasi Vande Bharat SleeperRoute and stopsThe second proposed service will connect Varanasi with New Delhi, passing through Prayagraj and Kanpur. The train is expected to provide another premium overnight travel option between eastern Uttar Pradesh and the national capital.The service is also expected to strengthen connectivity between Prayagraj, Delhi and other major cities along the route. For passengers travelling from Prayagraj to Delhi, it will offer an additional option alongside the Humsafar Express, Shiv Ganga Express and Prayagraj Express.The new service is expected to benefit pilgrims and tourists travelling to Varanasi, as well as businesspeople, working professionals and students from Prayagraj who need to reach the national capital early in the morning.TimingsAccording to the proposed schedule, train number 27421 will depart from Varanasi at 8.50pm and arrive at Prayagraj Junction at 10.35pm. Following a five-minute halt, it will leave Prayagraj at 10.40pm and reach Kanpur Central at 12.40am before arriving in New Delhi at 5.55am the following day.On the return journey, train number 27422 will depart from New Delhi at 9.40pm and reach Prayagraj at 4.45am the next day. After a five-minute halt, it will continue towards Varanasi, arriving at 6.45am.A special rake is scheduled to depart from Varanasi at 11am on the inaugural day. The railway administration is expected to announce the final timetable for regular operations soon. Once regular services commence, the Vande Bharat Sleeper is expected to run six days a week, except on Saturdays.Vande Bharat Sleeper fares: How much will tickets cost?The fare structure for Vande Bharat Sleeper trains is based on a per-passenger, per-kilometre rate.For the third air-conditioned class (3AC), the fare is Rs 2.40 per passenger per kilometre, excluding GST. The indicative fare for a journey of 1,000km in 3AC is Rs 2,400, excluding GST.The fare for Vande Bharat Sleeper trains ranges between Rs 2.40 and Rs 3.80 per passenger per kilometre (PKM). According to the information provided by the railways, this is lower than the fares of similar services in countries such as China, Japan and France, where the rates range from Rs 7 to Rs 20 per PKM.The railways has said it continues to operate different categories of train services to meet the travel needs of different sections of society. These include services with lower fares for underprivileged sections as well as trains offering enhanced facilities.The railways has also stated that Indian Railways' fares are among the lowest compared with those in other countries.Ticket booking: No RAC provision on Vande Bharat SleeperVande Bharat Sleeper trains are classified as a separate category of passenger service with an all-inclusive fare structure. There is no provision for Reservation Against Cancellation (RAC) tickets on these trains.Passengers on the waiting list can get confirmed tickets when passengers holding confirmed reservations cancel their tickets. The railways has said this arrangement allows the services to remain accessible to passengers.Facilities and reservation quotas for passengersThe reservation arrangements include earmarked lower berths for senior citizens, female passengers aged 45 years and above, and pregnant women.The combined quota will comprise six to seven lower berths per coach in Sleeper class, four to five lower berths per coach in air-conditioned three-tier (3AC), and three to four lower berths per coach in air-conditioned two-tier (2AC). The number of berths will depend on the number of coaches of each class in the train.The railways has also specified reservation quotas for persons with disabilities and their attendants in mail and express trains, including Rajdhani and Shatabdi-type services.The provisions include:Sleeper class: Four berths, comprising two lower and two middle berths.3AC/3E: Four berths, comprising two lower and two middle berths.Reserved second sitting (2S)/air-conditioned Chair Car (CC): Four seats in trains that have more than two coaches of the respective class.Food and catering arrangementsThe menu for the Mumbai-Bengaluru Vande Bharat Sleeper is being finalised in consultation with the Indian Railway Catering and Tourism Corporation (IRCTC), according to railway officials. Regional cuisines are expected to feature on board.The proposed sleeper configuration is intended to offer an alternative to air travel for passengers travelling between Mumbai and Bengaluru, while providing overnight connectivity on both routes.The country's first Vande Bharat Sleeper train was flagged off by PM Narendra Modi on January 17, 2026, on the Howrah-Kamakhya route. The service covers the distance between Howrah in West Bengal and Kamakhya in Assam in around 14 hours.The proposed Mumbai-Bengaluru and Varanasi-New Delhi services will expand the network of Vande Bharat Sleeper trains to additional routes.The details on fares, reservation provisions and train services were provided by Union minister for railways, information & broadcasting and electronics & information technology Ashwini Vaishnaw in a reply to questions in the Lok Sabha.You use AI every day. articles.title: Gas under Trump 2.0 is now more expensive than it was under Biden
articles.summary: On the campaign trail in 2024, Donald Trump promised to make gas dirt-cheap again and blamed record-high gas on the Biden-Harris “war on energy.”
articles.body: On the campaign trail in 2024, President Donald Trump promised to make gas dirt-cheap again and blamed record-high gas prices on the Biden-Harris “war on energy.” But then an actual war got in the way: Trump’s deeply unpopular conflict with Iran. Nearly eight months into a war that has destabilized the global energy system, the average price of gas during Trump’s second term is now more expensive than it was during the Biden era, according to a CNN analysis of AAA data. That milestone — a nearly unthinkable outcome as recently as January — underscores the frustration over high prices that has engulfed Trump and the Republican party leading up to the midterm elections. “It’s pretty astonishing,” Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, said of the fact that gas is now more expensive under Trump than former President Joe Biden. “I don’t think anyone would have predicted this 10 months ago.” It’s a major reversal of the return to sub-$2 gas that Trump promised in the summer of 2024 as he successfully convinced voters to return him to the White House. Polar opposite of Trump 1.0 During his first term, the national average for regular gas was just $2.47 a gallon. During the depths of the Covid-19 pandemic, gas prices plunged to as low as $1.77 nationally in April 2020. The health emergency caused demand for fuel to crash to the point that the world ran out of room to store oil, a phenomenon that briefly drove crude oil futures below zero for the first time ever. At one point in April 2020, Trump even pleaded with Saudi Arabia and Russia to stop pumping so much oil to halt a crash that threatened to bankrupt US oil companies and kill countless jobs. The situation couldn’t be more different today. The White House has waged a last-minute scramble to contain the damage from high fuel prices by taking a wide range of steps, including throwing farmers an $8 billion financial lifeline, buying millions of barrels of Russian diesel and examining steps to drive down extremely high shipping costs. “President Trump is fixing these long-term problems by taking tangible steps to increase our refining capacity here in the United States, while also taking immediate actions, such as releasing oil from our (Strategic Petroleum Reserve) to add supply to the market, temporarily waiving the Jones Act, and allowing red-dyed diesel for highway use, to lower prices at the pump,” White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers told CNN. Gas was cheap — before the war The outlook for gasoline and diesel prices was very favorable for Americans when the year started. Gas prices were safely below $3 a gallon, and, if anything, the energy market was worried about a supply glut that could keep fuel prices low. “If Trump really wanted to keep his promise to keep gas prices low, what he should have done was nothing,” said Gregory Brew, senior analyst at consulting firm Eurasia Group. “The market was oversupplied. There was a lot of crude sloshing around. Inventories were quite large. But Trump reversed that with the war.” Trump has argued that elevated gas prices are a small price to pay for keeping Iran from getting a nuclear weapon. But the spike in gas prices has angered voters who were hoping for the opposite under Trump. “High gas prices do not bode well for incumbents. They didn’t bode well for Biden either,” GasBuddy’s De Haan said. Stuck above $4 Gas prices spiked even higher under Biden, zooming to an all-time high of $5.02 a gallon in June 2022 after Russia invaded Ukraine. However, gas prices came down faster under Biden. In fact, 2026 has already shattered the Biden-era record for the most number of days with $4 gas or higher. The war with Iran led to the unthinkable: The unprecedented closure of the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway the world relied on to get oil out of the Middle East. While oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz have largely recovered, the cost to get that crude out has skyrocketed because of expensive and inefficient workarounds being used. The cost of hiring an oil tanker has skyrocketed from $65,000 a day last year to $1.6 million earlier this month. A shortage of refining Not only that, but the world is now grappling with a global refining shortage. Refineries that would normally churn out diesel, jet fuel and gasoline have been damaged in the Middle East and Russia. China has held back its own fuel exports. To make up for lost refinery output, the world has drawn fuel from commercial and emergency stockpiles. But that leaves the intricate energy system vulnerable to shocks. Case in point: A recent, unexpected outage at ExxonMobil’s Joliet, Illinois, refinery caused gasoline prices to go through the roof in Michigan, Ohio and other Great Lakes states in recent days. “Right now, there is no cushion. Commercial inventories are very low,” said Brew. “When there is any kind of outage, everyone starts to scramble.” Refiners, incentivized by the ability to make incredible profits due to the shortage, are producing as much fuel as possible even though normally this is the time of year operations slow for routine repairs. “Refiners have been running flat-out for months. If you own a refinery, you are printing money. Some are skipping maintenance because there is money to be made right now,” said Brew. “But if you run refiners for months on end, they will break down.” Once the Exxon refinery returns to normal, gas prices should come back down. However, that relief will likely be offset by the fact that oil prices have surged to seven-month highs as traders brace for the risk of a return to all-out war in the Middle East after the election. De Haan said Trump is “pulling every small lever he can” to cushion the blow from high prices. “Unfortunately, they’re not adding up to much,” he said. “Until the biggest lever — diplomacy — is pulled, he’s going to continue to fight against very elevated gas and record diesel. It’s fairly ominous.”

articles.title: AI is exposing how fragile the web really is. What you can do to stay safe
articles.summary: Keeping passwords secure and being wary of suspicious emails is more important than ever as hackers use sophisticated tools and AI to find the internet’s weak points.
articles.body: The vulnerabilities were around for years — more than a decade — but researchers were only able to understand how hackers could take advantage of them with the help of AI. The vulnerability, called P2PShell, impacts a coding language that powers 70% of the world’s websites, enabling hackers to remotely execute code or gain access to information stored on servers. That sent websites into a scramble to update their systems, with some government websites in Europe going offline temporarily this past week until they could install the fix. The discovery is yet another reminder of the fragile infrastructure of the internet. And with AI supercharging the abilities of both researchers and bad actors to discover flaws, it likely won’t be the last time a discovery like this is made. “A lot of the internet and a lot of global IT infrastructure runs on technology that’s quite old, or is based on things that are very old in terms of computers, and likely have similar vulnerabilities,” said Patrick Fussell, IBM’s global head of adversary simulation. With a vulnerability like P2PShell, there isn’t much that users can do to protect themselves. It’s up to organizations, businesses and governments to update their services with the latest security patches. But it does underscore the importance of being smart about your digital habits. The age-old advice of keeping your passwords secure and being wary of suspicious emails is more important than ever as hackers gain more sophisticated tools and use AI to find more of the internet’s weak points. Update your software Don’t ignore those software update notifications on your laptop or phone. Many of these updates include critical security fixes, and installing them as quickly as possible shortens the amount of time hackers have to take advantage of bugs. “Users still need to do their parts in terms of installing those updates and maintaining a good security hygiene to put them in a slightly better position,” said Gang Wang, associate professor of computer science at the University of Illinois. Most smartphones now support software updates for roughly seven years following their release. If you have an older phone, you should check if it’s still compatible with new software versions. You can find information about software compatibility on Apple, Google and Samsung’s websites. Watch out for phishing attacks Pay attention to the URLs of websites you’re visiting and links you’re clicking, especially if you’ve received the link in an email or text claiming to be your bank or credit card company. Never share personal data, email addresses, passwords, banking information or credit card numbers unless you’re certain the website is legitimate. AI has enabled attackers to create sophisticated phishing attacks that are more difficult to spot and may lack the key red flags of a scam. “The traditional way of determining a phishing attack was, ‘Hey, it didn’t sound right. It used wrong language. It had spelling errors, grammar errors,’” Jud Dressler, head of the risk operations center at cyber insurance firm Resilience, previously told CNN. “All of that stuff, the AI is going to take care of that.” AI can also help attackers conduct deeper research on potential targets to create more personalized and convincing messages, Dressler added. The best way to avoid phishing scams is to log into your account or call the company or person you’ve received a suspicious message from, rather than clicking links. Also, remember that smaller businesses may be slower to patch their systems in the event of an attack or data breach compared to large companies. Brush up on your passwords Never reuse passwords. Instead, try a password manager that creates long, unique passwords for all your online accounts. Simply put: Computers are better than humans at making passwords that are hard to guess. “We know humans, when they make decisions, they tend to make the same decisions as other people,” Rachel Tobac, CEO of cybersecurity and training company SocialProof Security, told CNN’s Terms of Service podcast with Clare Duffy in 2024. “So, you know, they make a password for their work. It has the work’s name in it. It’s got a capital letter in the first position to satisfy the capitalization requirement.” Tobac recommended password managers like Bitwarden, 1Password and Dashlane. The most important thing to look for is whether a password manager offers encryption, which keeps your passwords safe and unreadable to hackers. Other tips for staying safe online Use passkeys instead of passwords: Passkeys are digital credentials that let you sign into online services using your fingerprint, face scan or PIN instead of a typed password. Passkeys are generally thought to be more secure than passwords since they’re tied to biometric data stored on your device that can’t be as easily stolen or spoofed. Apple, Google and Microsoft’s operating systems all support passkeys. Use two-factor authentication: Enable two-factor verification on any service that offers it. Two-factor authentication sends a login code via text, email or phone call as an extra layer of protection in addition to your password. Some experts prefer app-based code generators like Google Authenticator since text messages can be vulnerable to hackers. Monitor all your important accounts: Keep an eye on all important accounts for suspicious changes. Many offer automatic email or text alerts. Freeze your credit report: Freezing your credit file with the three main agencies — Experian, Transunion and Equifax — is an easy way to prevent nefarious actors from trying to open new accounts in your name. Create a family code word: If you get a suspicious call or message from someone who sounds like a loved one asking for information, call them back yourself, or call people close to them if you can’t get a hold of them. A code word shared between you and your loved ones can confirm their identity. While AI is making it easier for even novice hackers to execute more advanced campaigns, bad actors are still trying to take advantage of humans at the end of the day. “It’s still kind of a familiar attack method,” said Dressler. “It’s just using essentially AI to make it more believable and more effective.”

articles.title: The markets are starting to act seriously weird. Blame AI
articles.summary: AI’s shaky balance sheets raise questions about circular financing that investors have long questioned but the industry and many traders have swept under the rug.
articles.body: On the surface, the markets seem stable. Stocks are near record highs, and bonds are right about where they’ve been for the past couple of months. But check under the hood, and you’ll see signs that investors are growing increasingly nervous — mostly because of AI. This time, the anxiety isn’t because AI is going to kill us all (that was SO last month). The latest concern: AI may be a financial quagmire. And if the air is starting to come out of the AI bubble, it could threaten to knock over the foundation supporting America’s economic boom. The weird stuff The stock market is so big and diverse that it’s sometimes useful for investors to measure it in creative ways, comparing two measurements to figure out if there’s a trend that the headline numbers can’t show you. For example, you can measure the benchmark S&P 500 stock index in a number of ways. The most common way is to weight each stock by its market value — giving gigantic tech companies worth trillions of dollars considerable influence over the ups and downs of the stock market. But if you look at the S&P 500 another way, weighting each stock equally, you can sometimes get a clearer picture of how the market is performing across industries. Equally weighting stocks ensures companies in smaller industries aren’t drowned out by massive ones, like Big Tech. When comparing those two measurements on October 22, the result was seriously bizarre — so strange it had only happened twice before in the past three decades. The main index, weighted by market value, fell 1.2%. But the equal-weighted index gained 0.5%. Since 1995, that massive divergence in the two measurements had happened only twice before: April 14, 1999, and March 30, 2000, noted James Reilly, senior markets economist at Capital Economics. What does it mean? A clue can be found in another weird thing that happened that same day. Also on Thursday, the 10-year Treasury yield slammed on the brakes and went into reverse, falling below 5% and tumbling in the largest single-day decline since March 10, 2023 — the day that Silicon Valley Bank imploded. So investors were pouring money out of tech and into Treasuries and non-tech stocks at a historic pace. It’s a sign that AI is making some folks on Wall Street kind of nervous. What changed? Bonds had been tumbling (and yields, as a result, had been surging to multi-decade highs) for three core reasons: The Iran war sent inflation on a serious rebound, cutting off the world’s oil and fuel supplies and sending prices through the roof. Bond investors, when confronted with rebounding inflation, demanded higher yields to compensate for the chunk of their investment that inflation has been eating into. Meanwhile, America’s debt has skyrocketed to $40 trillion, and its budget deficit surged to $2 trillion over the past fiscal year. Politicians across the political spectrum continue to advocate for populist policies, including lower taxes and higher spending, giving investors no hope for a wave of fiscal responsibility soon to take over Washington. That means Treasury will need to keep borrowing — a lot, flooding the market with bonds. And enormous AI investment has underpinned America’s sustained economic growth in recent years. But the infrastructure needed to power AI is expensive — around $1 trillion a year and growing. Tech companies are borrowing huge amounts of money from investors, in the form of bonds, crowding out demand for other debt, including Treasuries. None of this has fundamentally changed. In fact, the Iran war, inflation and the debt problems are potentially about to get even worse. Oil prices are at four-year highs, and fuel prices are exploding higher in some parts of the United States. And President Donald Trump has signaled the costly Iran war is about to kick into high gear again after the midterms. Even with that backdrop, government bonds, which investors have turned their backs on for months, suddenly grew popular again. Investors recently started asking some serious questions about the AI part of this three-legged stool that had been supporting bond yields. That wobbly AI leg made folks worried. And when traders feel nervous, they come running home for safety. And the safest home on the planet offers the security of the US dollar and Treasuries. What’s wrong with AI? If we are in the midst of a paradigm shift, the turning point may have begun with CoreWeave. The neocloud company, which rents out computing power to AI companies, is fueled by debt. Its borrowing costs ballooned to an astounding 15% earlier this month as investors grew concerned about its financial prospects. That dwarfs its rate of return on its investments. In other words: CoreWeave is losing a ton of money and may not be able to pay off its debt. CoreWeave may be an outlier — or it may not be. A Wall Street Journal report on Anthropic’s draft IPO filing showed a nearly $81 billion loss in the first half of 2026 — on pace to dwarf the record for the largest-ever annual loss reported by a public company (if Anthropic goes public this year). Meta reported that it spent $2 billion more cash than it produced in the third quarter, sending its stock tumbling 7% Thursday. AI’s shaky balance sheets raised questions about that whole circular financing thing that investors have long questioned but the industry and many traders have swept under the rug. If every tech company is invested in every tech company, is this all just a highly leveraged house of cards? And what happens when one of those cards falls? So some traders are pausing to re-think how much value Wall Street has been placing on AI — and whether these debt levels are sustainable. “What we’re seeing is elevated volatility around something that looks and feels and smells like a bubble,” said Joe Brusuelas, chief economist for RSM US. What’s not clear is how long this AI fizzle-out will last. The Nasdaq is in the midst of a two-week-long, 6% slide, but we’ve been down this road before, with investors growing nervous around past earnings seasons that tech companies are spending too much on AI — only to pour money back into AI stocks when some companies report signs of sustained demand. And even if the AI bubble popped, it wouldn’t necessarily mean the economy would go down with it, Reilly noted. Each financial bubble has its own distinct character. In recent years, economists have described the economy as in a “rolling recession,” as various sectors boomed and others busted, balancing one another out and preventing the entire economy from entering a downturn. This time may be the same. Or different. No one knows. So the market went a little haywire. Bond yields tumbled. And the stock market did something it has done only three times since 1995. It may be the start of something –– or it may be just another bump in the road.

articles.summary: MUMBAI: State Bank of India (SBI) expects interest rates to rise by 50 basis points in December, with chairman CS Setty saying higher rates could affect
articles.body: MUMBAI: State Bank of India (SBI) expects interest rates to rise by 50 basis points in December, with chairman CS Setty saying higher rates could affect discretionary consumption credit demand but were unlikely to significantly dent overall credit growth given 7.1% growth forecasted for the economy.“Interest rates will influence the composition and quantum of credit demand, not immediately,” Setty said at the Business Standard BFSI Summit. “We need to distinguish between weakening of demand and moderation of credit growth. We are coming from a phase of robust growth in credit. While discretionary consumption demand could be affected, I do not think credit for productive activities will be impacted,” he said.Setty said he did not expect system-wide concerns over credit quality, although individual borrowers could face stress from higher interest rates.On deposits, Setty said household savings were undergoing a structural shift, with households increasingly practising asset allocation, even if they were not fully conscious of it. “There is only so much that rates can propel you in deposit mobilization. What matters is service quality,” he said, adding that the ease of moving funds from savings accounts to term deposits had improved significantly.“The liquidity RBI has been providing and the FCNR flows will ensure that there is no rate-driven competition for deposits,” he said. Stock market movements could trigger some shifts in household savings, but interest rates alone had limited ability to drive deposit mobilisation.On the MDR on UPI Setty said the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) had transformed India's payment system and become a global success story, but rising transaction volumes required substantial investment in technology, computing capacity and risk management.SBI handles 40 crore daily UPI transactions, with real-time monitoring of transactions above Rs 5,000 requiring investment in computing and risk management. Chairman CS Setty said minimum MDR would help fund payment rails, with 98% of transactions excluded and consumer impact lower than projected. Transaction-level monitoring should limit cost pass-through to consumers.YONO, designed to cut transaction costs, has 7 crore registered users. SBI aims to bring 30 crore customers, including third-party UPI users, onto YONO by 2030 through YONO Bharat, focused on financial inclusion. Device-neutral access and simpler services could follow in six to seven months.SBI’s AI/ML portfolio stands at Rs 1 lakh crore. Generative AI in knowledge management and cheque clearing has cut processing centres from 17 to four, improving efficiency and enabling workforce redeployment. articles.title: Who is Lula? From ex-worker and prisoner to Brazil's president again
articles.summary: The firebrand left-winger, who has at times been at odds with Trump, has won his fourth term as Brazil's president.
articles.body:
On the face of it, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has done the impossible one more time - within three weeks he overturned defeat in first-round voting to gain re-election as Brazil's president.

It was no mean achievement for a man who before his first successful run at the post in 2002 had tried three times unsuccessfully.

When he became president in 2003, he came to office as the first leftist leader of Brazil in nearly half a century.

Now aged 80 and with plenty of experience at governing as large a democracy as Brazil, he has bucked the trend of electoral victory for right-wing leaders in Latin America whose policies mirror that of US President Donald Trump.

Lula's first presidential victory in 2002 marked the end of an unprecedented journey from poverty.

The son of a poor, illiterate peasant family, Lula worked as a peanut seller and shoe-shine boy as a child, only learning to read when he was 10 years old.

He went on to train as a metalworker and found work in an industrial city near São Paulo, where he lost the little finger of his left hand in an accident in the 1960s.

Lula was not initially interested in politics, but threw himself into trade union activism.

Elected leader of the 100,000-strong Metalworkers' Union in 1975, he transformed trade union activism in Brazil by turning what had mostly been government-friendly organisations into a powerful independent movement.

In 1980, Lula brought together a combination of trade unionists, intellectuals, Trotskyites and Church activists to found the Workers' Party (PT), the first major socialist party in the country's history.

The PT went on to gradually replace its revolutionary commitment to changing the power structure in Brazil with a more pragmatic, social democratic platform.

Lula came to power promising major reforms to the country's political and economic system.

He vowed to eradicate hunger and create a self-confident, caring, outward-looking nation.

In his time in office, Lula pumped billions of dollars into social programmes and can reasonably claim to have helped reverse Brazil's historic inequalities.

By increasing the minimum wage well above the rate of inflation and broadening state help to the most impoverished with a family grant programme, the Bolsa Familia, he helped some 44 million people and cemented his support among the poor.

However, many commentators argue that the programme failed to address the structural problems that underpin poverty, such as a lack of education.

He left office eight years later, after serving two terms as president, enjoying exceptionally high popularity ratings for a retiring Latin American leader - 83% - having raised Brazil's profile on the international scene and presided over the longest period of economic growth in three decades.

Unable to run for a third term, Lula left the presidency and, shortly afterwards, was diagnosed with throat cancer. He even shaved his trademark beard during treatment. Doctors declared him cured of the disease in 2012.

Lula wins fourth term in dramatic Brazil election comeback

Lula faces hostile congress and divided country after Brazil election win

Under his chosen successor, progress stalled. The economic boom also gave way to recession, and the country's political scene was rocked by a huge investigation into top-level corruption, known as Operation Car Wash.

Lula was among those to get caught up in the scandal. In July 2017, he was convicted of corruption and sentenced to more than nine years in prison for accepting a beachside flat as a bribe from engineering firm OAS - a sentence increased on appeal to 12 years.

Lula was also jailed for 12 years and 11 months for corruption and money laundering for receiving bribes from two construction and engineering firms by way of funding improvements in a country house he and his family used.

He has always maintained his innocence, insisting accusations against him were politically motivated.

In 2019, he was released after having served just over 18 months, after a Supreme Court ruling that the incarceration had been illegal, having come before all appeals had been exhausted.

Those convictions were annulled in 2021, leaving Lula free to run for a third term in 2022, beating right-winger Jair Bolsonaro.

When he re-entered office in 2023, he vowed it would be his last term, and yet his party endorsed him as their candidate again this year, even though he will turn 81 on Tuesday.

Even backers of the PT will acknowledge that he achieved more in his first two terms - from January 2003 to December 2010 - than in his most recent four years in office.

And while his supporters described him ahead of the 2022 election as the "saviour of the Amazon", praising his commitment to protecting the rainforest, some environmentalists have been critical of some of his recent actions.

His support for exploratory oil drilling in offshore waters near the mouth of the Amazon in particular has drawn criticism.

Lula insists that he remains committed to eventually phasing out fossil fuels and argues that oil revenues are key to financing Brazil's transition to clean energy.

His government has also pointed to the reduction in deforestation in the Amazon - satellite data suggests the area deforested in the first half of 2026 was reduced to its lowest in the past decade - as proof that its policies were working.

Lula's third term coincided with the return to office of Trump.

The two men represent different ends of the political spectrum and have found it impossible not to voice their differences in public.

Even though the US has a trade surplus with Brazil, Donald Trump imposed 50% tariffs on Brazilian goods in July that year, citing the trial on coup charges of Brazil's right-wing former president Jair Bolsonaro as a trigger. Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year jail sentence and it was his son, Flávio, who Lula beat in Sunday's election run-off.

Lula accused Trump of foreign interference and said "he's not emperor of the world". But their relationship improved after a White House in May this year, after which the two leaders exchanged public compliments - Trump called Lula "dynamic", while the Brazilian president said he left the meeting "very satisfied".

In July of this year, the US imposed 25% tariffs on most goods from Brazil.

The two governments still disagree on key issues such as crime, and Lula acknowledged they are especially far apart on trade.

Referring to what Trump has dubbed the "Donroe doctrine" - his administration's national security strategy which asserts that US dominance in the Western hemisphere should not be interfered with - Lula has insisted that "Brazil does not fit into anyone's backyard".

Lula has criticised the fact that five countries - the permanent members of the UN Security Council - have the power to veto decisions and argued that this tilted the balance in favour of those who won World War Two, excluding nations representing billions of people like Brazil, Germany, India, and Japan, as well as African countries.

Brazil is an active member of the Brics - a grouping that unites Brazil with Russia, India, China and South Africa.

Lula defends his continued alliances with Russia and China and sees the Brics as an emerging counterweight to the West.

He has defended his choice to continue to purchase Russian oil while Russia wages war in Ukraine.

articles.title: Verizon beats profit estimates, raises guidance
articles.summary: Investing.com -- Verizon Communications Inc. (NYSE: VZ) reported its third-quarter results before the open today, topping profit expectations.
articles.body:
Investing.com -- Verizon Communications Inc. (NYSE: VZ) reported its third-quarter results before the open today, topping profit expectations.

Adjusted earnings per share of $1.31 beat the analyst estimate of $1.28 by $0.03. Revenue came in at $34.31 billion, up 1.5% YoY, but fell short of the consensus estimate of $34.77 billion. The company raised its full-year 2026 adjusted EPS guidance to $5.04-$5.06, with a midpoint of $5.05 that exceeds the analyst consensus of $5.02.

The telecommunications company delivered 406,000 postpaid phone net additions, representing an increase of more than 820% YoY and marking the strongest third-quarter performance in five years.

Verizon added 137,000 postpaid net accounts, its best performance in over a decade. Mobility and broadband service revenue reached $23.5 billion, growing 2.9% YoY. The company also reported consolidated adjusted EBITDA of $13.8 billion, up 8.0% YoY, which it described as the highest quarterly result ever reported.

Shares rose 0.7% following the announcement.

"Verizon delivered another record-breaking quarter. One year into our transformation, Verizon is fundamentally stronger — operationally, financially, and competitively," said Dan Schulman, Verizon CEO. "By prioritizing customer-first offerings like Simplicity and our expanded loyalty program over heavy subsidies, we are winning loyal, high-value customers while expanding margins, reducing churn, and generating strong sustained cash flow."

For the full year 2026, Verizon raised its guidance for the third consecutive quarter. The company now expects postpaid phone net additions of 1.1 million to 1.2 million, up from the upper half of 750,000 to 1.0 million. Adjusted EPS is projected to grow 7.0% to 7.5% YoY, up from the prior range of 6.0% to 7.0%. Free cash flow is expected to approach 12.0% growth YoY, up from 9.0% to 10.0%.

Cash flow from operations was $11.5 billion for the quarter, up 2.2% YoY, while free cash flow reached $7.8 billion, up 12.1% YoY.

articles.title: This warning sign suggests more tech stock poundings could be in the cards
articles.summary: Don't ignore the message from the bond market, tech investors.
articles.body:
The tech trade could have some sharper down days ahead if the red flags in the bond market are to be believed.

Hyperscaler credit default swaps continue to widen, BTIG strategist Jonathan Krinsky pointed out. Investment-grade tech credit default swaps are now the widest they've been since 2022.

Yet, the S&P Tech Sector is just a few percentage points below its highs — essentially shrugging off the worries being expressed in the bond market.

A credit default swap (CDS) acts as insurance against a corporate borrower defaulting on its debt. When a CDS spread widens, buying that default insurance becomes pricier. It means institutional credit investors perceive higher credit risk, worsening balance sheet health, or rising debt loads.

The backdrop for tech stocks has become increasingly choppy in October.

Concerns began earlier this month with neocloud company CoreWeave ( CRWV ).

The company's corporate bonds across maturities continued to be dumped amid fears of an AI slowdown and its implications for the company's precarious balance sheet. That has triggered a subsequent sharp sell-off in the stock.

CoreWeave stock has been crushed by 35% in October.

Meta ( META ) then dropped a bombshell in its third quarter results last week, posting negative free cash flow for the first time since 2012 amid aggressive spending on AI.

On Friday, the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) closed below last Friday's low — a red flag to chart watchers.

"The reality, of course, is that it is hard to identify the exact trigger for an AI crash. But we can model the fallout. In terms of financial markets, the impact is likely to be sizable," TS Lombard strategist Dario Perkins warned in a new note . "US stocks would be hit hard, with (at least) a 30% decline. That would wipe out around $20 trillion in market cap."

Across debt markets and private credits, he estimated "$125–200 billion in losses. Spreads would blow out, and we should expect a wave of tech-related defaults."

articles.title: $58 billion in SNAP, SSI and Medicare benefits go unclaimed by older adults — how retirees can save thousands
articles.summary: Navigating different government programs can be overwhelming, but there are agencies that can help older adults access the benefits they need.
articles.body:
Millions of low-income older adults in America are missing out on benefits that could help them cover costs for medical bills, groceries, utility bills and more.

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP

A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change

Data from the National Council on Aging (NCOA) show that more than 9 million older adults who are eligible for benefits are not claiming them.

Collectively, NCOA says that an estimated $58 billion in benefits that could help to pay for daily essentials are being left on the table.

The NCOA says that many older adults may incorrectly believe that they don't qualify for these benefits programs, while others may not even know they exist

For those low-income older adults who aren't collecting benefits they're eligible for, the dollar amounts being left on the table are significant.

The NCOA data looks at three benefit programs: the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), Supplemental Security Income (SSI) and Medicare Savings Programs (MSPs).

Just 38% of eligible individuals age 65+ participated in SNAP in 2023, the NCOA found. That means an estimated 9.1 million eligible people didn't claim benefits that could have helped them put food on the table.

That's $188 a month, or $2,256 a year, in SNAP benefits that people are missing out on (based on the 2023 average benefit amount for households with a 60+ adult).

For SSI, 40% of those eligible participated in 2023, meaning 3.6 million people left those benefits on the table. That amounts to $552.29 a month, or $6,627.48 a year, based on the December 2023 average for adults 65+.

And for MSPs, which help cover Medicare premiums, deductibles and co-insurance, 49% of those eligible claimed benefits, meaning 6.6 million people weren't enrolled. That's $164.90 a month unclaimed, or $1,978.80 a year, based on the standard Part B premium for 2023.

All told, for someone who qualified for all three benefits programs, based on 2023 benefit levels, that's $10,862.28 a year to help cover life's essentials.

There's other help for low-income older adults available as well. Those who qualify for the Medicare Savings Program, and those who receive SSI, also automatically qualify for the Extra Help program , which helps pay for Medicare drug coverage (Part D) and other costs.

articles.title: The 10 biggest stocks are faltering, and it's dragging the S&P 500 down
articles.summary: The markets have seen a downward bias for months, in large part because of the biggest stocks.
articles.body:
Apple ( AAPL ) and Nvidia ( NVDA ) may be renewing their battle for the world's most valuable company, but a challenging few months for the S&P 500's ( ^GSPC ) 10 largest companies are holding back the broader index.

The 10 biggest stocks in the S&P 500 have started to falter again relative to the rest of the market, RBC strategist Lori Calvasina rightly pointed out in a new note. These 10 stocks include Apple, Nvidia, Amazon ( AMZN ), Broadcom ( AVGO ), the two classes of Alphabet ( GOOGL ) ( GOOG ) stock, Micron ( MU ), Meta ( META ), Microsoft ( MSFT ), and Tesla ( TSLA ).

Their stutter step weighs on the overall stock market given their weight in the benchmark index.

Calvasina said she remains on the sidelines with tech, which she downgraded to a Market Weight rating earlier this month.

Mounting investor skepticism about the timeline for AI return on investment has triggered severe rotation and pullbacks in megacap tech, preventing the broader market from breaking out.

Consider this: Former market leader Nvidia is down about 13% from its all-time highs, while Tesla is off by 26%. Double-digit declines relative to their highs are also in play for Amazon, Alphabet, Google and SpaceX.

The latest earnings from Meta and SpaceX only fanned investors' fears, with each reporting negative free cash flow and outlining aggressive AI spending plans.

Amid rising oil prices and portfolio de-risking ahead of November's midterm elections, institutional investors have remained in a "wait-and-see" mode rather than chasing stocks near all-time highs.

"We've been max Overweight stocks and max Underweight sovereign bonds since mid-March. Given the constant narrative bingo we just can't have the same level of conviction any longer. Heading into the mid-terms there may well be worries about AI regulation in the event of a 'Blue Wave' as well as renewed geopolitical concerns around the Middle East," HSBC strategist Max Kettner wrote in a new note on Monday.

Kettner said he is moving to the sidelines on stocks near term.

articles.title: Gonzalo Bernardos, economista, sobre la propuesta de Países Bajos de ceder la vivienda social a los inmigrantes: "Deben tener los mismos derechos y deberes"
articles.standfirst: Bernardos critica la postura de la ministra de Vivienda del país neerlandés, que ha defendido que muchos jóvenes pueden seguir viviendo con sus familias
articles.summary: Bernardos critica la postura de la ministra de Vivienda del país neerlandés, que ha defendido que muchos jóvenes pueden seguir viviendo con sus familias
articles.body: La crisis de la vivienda ha abierto un nuevo frente de debate en los Países Bajos. La propuesta de la ministra de Vivienda, Elanor Boekholt-O’Sullivan, ha generado polémica tras defender que muchos jóvenes que buscan independizarse todavía pueden permanecer en casa de sus padres, mientras el país afronta la necesidad de encontrar alojamiento para las personas que han obtenido autorización para residir en su territorio. Las declaraciones han provocado críticas por la prioridad que reciben determinados colectivos en el acceso a las viviendas sociales. La situación ha llegado al debate político neerlandés, donde se cuestiona cómo compatibilizar las necesidades de los jóvenes que llevan años esperando una vivienda con las obligaciones de alojamiento de las personas refugiadas. El economista Gonzalo Bernardos también se ha pronunciado sobre esta controversia y ha defendido que los inmigrantes deben contar con los mismos derechos y deberes que los españoles, “pero ni más ni menos”. Su crítica se centra en lo que considera una diferencia de trato entre quienes buscan acceder a una vivienda y quienes pueden beneficiarse de determinadas medidas de prioridad. La cuestión se originó después de que la ministra neerlandesa señalara que muchos jóvenes que buscan su primera vivienda “pueden vivir con sus padres”. La respuesta llegó en un contexto de escasez de vivienda asequible y largas listas de espera para acceder al alquiler social. Bernardos considera que esta situación plantea un problema de igualdad de trato. “Para mí, los inmigrantes deben tener los mismos derechos y deberes que los españoles, pero ni más ni menos”, sostiene el economista, que cuestiona que las necesidades de quienes buscan independizarse queden en un segundo plano frente a las de los recién llegados. La controversia no se limita a las declaraciones de la ministra. Representantes políticos neerlandeses han pedido explicaciones sobre qué grupo debe tener prioridad cuando la oferta de vivienda es insuficiente. También se han planteado preguntas parlamentarias sobre las dificultades de los jóvenes que llevan años en listas de espera y no pueden iniciar una vida independiente. El Gobierno neerlandés defiende la necesidad de encontrar alternativas para alojar a las personas con permiso de residencia, mientras continúa el debate sobre la asignación de viviendas sociales. La falta de oferta y el aumento de la demanda han convertido el acceso a un hogar en uno de los principales desafíos del país. Para Bernardos, el criterio fundamental debe ser la igualdad entre ciudadanos e inmigrantes, sin que un colectivo tenga más derechos que otro. La discusión neerlandesa vuelve así a poner sobre la mesa una cuestión que también preocupa en otros países europeos: cómo repartir unos recursos habitacionales limitados sin dejar atrás a quienes llevan años intentando acceder a una vivienda.

articles.title: Anthropic reveals $80 billion loss, huge spending spree ahead of IPO
articles.summary: Artificial intelligence startup Anthropic unveils its first public IPO filing ahead of what is expected to be one of the largest stock debuts in history.
articles.body: Artificial intelligence startup Anthropic on Monday unveiled its public IPO filing ahead of what is expected to be one of the largest stock debuts in history. That offering, widely expected to come sometime in mid-November, could value the Claude developer at more than $2 trillion. That could surpass the current record holder, Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which raised $75 billion in an IPO in June that valued the rocket-AI-social-media firm at $2.1 trillion. The filing did not include a potential share price, the number of shares to be offered or a valuation for the whole company, all of which will be determined after Anthropic holds a “road show” with investors, prospective investors and its bankers. Monday’s filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission showed that Anthropic, like other AI firms, is splashing out unprecedented amounts of cash on cloud services to run its AI models. The company plans to spend at least $110 billion with Amazon for cloud services through April 2036 and another $120 billion with SpaceX through 2029. Anthropic also said it planned to spend $115 billion with Google and $45 billion with Microsoft, both through 2033, for computing infrastructure. The filing said that the company recorded revenue growth of “1,368% year over year for the three months ended June 30, 2026.” The cost of renting servers and chips grew by 300% over the same period. Anthropic’s net loss for the first six months of 2026 was $80.7 billion. For the entirety of 2025, the company reported a $42 billion net loss. Anthropic added that it expects its current cash and sales to be sufficient for the next 12 months but warned that future revenue growth depends on a number of important factors, including the cost of infrastructure. As a result, it said, “we may be required to seek additional financing sooner than we currently anticipate.” The company said it has raised about $141 billion of capital through the end of June and is sitting on $112.4 billion of cash. The company plans to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol “ANT.” Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are leading the historic offering, as they did with SpaceX’s record deal. But already, the offering is coming slightly later than expected as recent market moves give investors pause about the trajectory of the seemingly ever-expanding AI boom. Monday’s filing is unlikely to calm those fears. Alongside its dramatic spending and borrowing figures, Anthropic warned that it “may not generate sufficient revenue to achieve or sustain profitability in the future.” “While we have experienced significant revenue growth in recent periods, our business is highly capital intensive,” the company said. “Our revenue growth may not be sustainable, and our rate of growth may decrease.” Nevertheless, Anthropic told regulators and investors that it plans to keep burning through capital: “We expect our costs will increase over time and our losses will continue as we expect to invest significant resources towards growing our business and operating as a public company.” On Sunday, a top Wall Street economist warned that the sector had yet to deliver broad gains to the wider economy. “Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech,” said Torsten Slok, chief economist at investment firm Apollo Global Management. “Profit margins are rising for the Mag 7 but are flat for the S&P 493,” he wrote Sunday, referring to the companies left in the benchmark S&P 500 after subtracting Meta, Microsoft, Alphabet, Apple, Amazon, Nvidia and Tesla. “And there are still no signs of AI boosting productivity growth.” The Nasdaq 100, which tracks the largest public AI developers, is up 15% this year. That’s more than the broader S&P 500’s 11% gain so far this year. Market jitters over potential cracks in the AI boom have also caused a number of smaller IPOs to put their plans on hold. Earlier this month, a number of small offerings delayed or canceled their plans to go public, citing “market conditions.” But still, the largest AI companies continue to raise massive amounts of funding for their projects. On Monday, Meta Platforms announced an up to $95 billion stock offering, while SpaceX said it had secured $40 billion in funding to buy Nvidia graphics processing units, which it called the largest type of fundraising ever. As part of every stock offering, companies are asked to outline risks and uncertainties facing their businesses. Some of the risk factors outlined by Anthropic included safety, reliable computing infrastructure and its ability to “navigate an evolving, uncertain, and at times divergent global regulatory landscape.” “Concerns have been raised both within our organization and by other researchers, regulators, policymakers, and industry participants that sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity,” the filing said. Some of those potential risks have manifested themselves recently, as the firms have faced intense scrutiny over a swath of incidents in which their models and agents have hacked into government and private websites and services. The companies, including Anthropic, have said they’re taking steps to bolster security. But those incidents also came as Anthropic co-founder Dario Amodei wrote in September that companies should “pace the frontier,” a way of saying that AI models were advancing faster than humans could grasp their capabilities. Some within the industry conditionally agreed with Amodei, but Washington sharply rebuked the idea. He and President Donald Trump met privately and again at an industry meeting that took place at the White House. Trump later said he wanted no holds at all placed on the progress the industry is making. Trump and the leaders of Google, Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI, Nvidia and SpaceX signed what Trump said was a “morally binding” agreement to police AI safety. “Look, I say, if you’re going to seek regulation, they can put you out of business,” Trump told Time magazine earlier this year. “But my attitude is, we’re winning against the world by a lot, and I want to keep winning.”

articles.title: Trading on Brazil's stock exchange halted following Lula reelection
articles.summary: By Rodrigo Campos, Marcela Ayres and Karin Strohecker NEW YORK/BRASILIA/LONDON, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Brazil's stock exchange halted trading via a circuit break...
articles.body:
By Rodrigo Campos, Marcela Ayres and Karin Strohecker

NEW YORK/BRASILIA/LONDON, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Brazil's stock exchange halted trading via a circuit breaker safety mechanism on Monday in the wake of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's reelection, undoing bullish investor sentiment after his right-wing rival led the first round of voting earlier in the month.

The real ‌weakened around 12% against the US dollar in spot trading as trading in Brazil got underway and Bovespa stock index futures tumbled nearly 15%, while interest rate ‌futures rose sharply. The selloff extended to Brazil's international bonds, with longer-dated debt hit hardest and the 2056 maturity down nearly 3 cents.

Trading on Brazil's stock exchange was halted for 30 minutes after the benchmark Ibovespa index fell 10% ​from its previous close, triggering the market's circuit breaker mechanism, stock exchange operator B3 said in a statement.

The move came after B3 had initially expanded the daily trading limits for Ibovespa stock index futures, dollar futures and interest rate futures in response to heightened market volatility.

As Brazilian markets haemorrhaged, the country's Treasury cancelled its regular auctions of inflation-linked and fixed-rate government bonds scheduled for October 27 and October 29, respectively.

The collapse is a sharp reversal from the rally seen earlier this month, when markets soared on expectations of a shift to the right after Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former ‌President Jair Bolsonaro, unexpectedly finished first in the opening round ⁠of Brazil's presidential elections.

Stocks closed on Friday almost 7% above their level before the first round, while the real was nearly 5% stronger against the US dollar.

Interest rate futures had also reflected expectations that tighter fiscal policy under Flavio Bolsonaro would allow borrowing costs to decline.

Prediction markets had pointed ⁠to a Bolsonaro win, with Kalshi pricing in a more than 75% chance of that outcome on Friday.

"We expect a sharp market reaction on Monday, with aggressive repricing, a selloff in assets and interest rate futures likely to hit their upper limit shortly after the open," said Luis Felipe Vital, head of macro strategy at Warren Investimentos.

Bolsonaro's refusal to concede and his pledge to seek an annulment added to ​investor ​uncertainty.

"Important for local financial markets will be how quickly Bolsonaro accepts the result – or at least allows ​the constitution to run its course," said Chris Turner, strategist at ING ‌in London.

articles.title: Anthropic publicly files IPO prospectus, noting strong revenue growth and massive spending
articles.summary: Anthropic has filed its S-1 investment prospectus with the SEC, giving investors a look at the company's most important financial information ahead of its IP...
articles.body:
Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) has publicly filed its S-1 investment prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission, giving investors a look at the company's most important financial information ahead of its initial public offering.

The company, which will trade under the ticker symbol ANT, said it generated $16.3 billion in revenue in the six-month period that ended in June, more than the $4.6 billion the company saw in all of 2025.

But the company also spent $9 billion on AI infrastructure in the first six months of the year, ahead of the $7.3 billion it spent throughout 2025.

Anthropic's IPO filing reveals $430 billion in locked-in AI computing

Anthropic plans to go public at a time when AI tokens have never been cheaper

How this Anthropic investor is thinking through its IPO filing

Roughly one-fifth of Anthropic's revenue came from two customers. The remainder came from a small handful of clients.

According to the S-1, Anthropic saw a net loss of $80.7 billion through June, though the vast majority of that was the result of accounting charges.

The AI giant also plans to spend upward of $430 billion on locked-in cloud computing deals with companies including Amazon and Google, major Anthropic investors, and others in the years ahead. Toss in cancellable and smaller deals, the total reaches as much as $637 billion.

The company's market debut will test investors' appetite for a second public listing by a firm with an already massive valuation. SpaceX ( SPCX ) went public on June 12 at $150 per share and ended the day 20% higher.

Helmed by CEO Dario Amodei , who co-founded the company with his sister Daniela, the company's president, Anthropic established a strong foothold in the enterprise market with its Claude chatbot, the popular AI coding tool Claude Code, and Claude Cowork.

But the S-1 also reveals Anthropic's fears that models may develop capabilities the company doesn't anticipate.

The filing lays out a host of potentially damaging scenarios in which its AI models could cause real-world harm. Anthropic said that could limit the company's ability to cover any potential damages.

In an early September essay, Amodei called on the AI industry to slow the development of frontier AI models over fears that they could become too powerful for humans to control. The piece, coupled with statements by former and current researchers at AI companies, sent shockwaves through the industry and raised concerns that the technology could "kill all humans."

Experts dispute those claims, saying that the risks surrounding AI stem from basic cybersecurity protections and from preventing people and governments from using it for things like identity theft, discrimination, and labor displacement.

articles.title: Brazilian stocks plunge after Lula's surprising election victory
articles.summary: Brazilian stocks plunged in early trading on Monday after the country's surprising runoff election results reversed a rally earlier this month in Brazilian a...
articles.body:
Brazilian stocks plunged in early trading Monday after the country's surprising runoff election results reversed a rally earlier this month in Brazilian assets.

The president of Latin America's largest economy, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, secured a surprising win over right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro in a Sunday runoff election after Bolsonaro took an unexpected first-round lead in the general election earlier this month.

The iShares MSCI Brazil ETF ( EWZ ), which tracks Brazilian stocks, dropped 24% early Monday, a move that, if sustained through the closing bell, could mark the index's biggest single-day decline since it began trading in July 2000, according to Yahoo Finance data. The ETF's previous record was a 23% decline at the beginning of the pandemic in March 2020.

The stocks of majority state-owned Brazilian energy giant Petrobras ( PBR ) and Nu Holdings ( NU ), the parent company of Brazilian digital bank Nubank, fell 15% and 20%, respectively.

Earlier this month, Brazilian stocks surged following Bolsonaro's better-than-expected showing in the country's Oct. 4 general election.

Investors viewed Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, as a candidate poised to shift the country toward more business-friendly and fiscally constrained policies.

The election outcome comes after polls showed Bolsonaro holding a narrow lead over President Lula, while wagers on the prediction market Kalshi suggested the right-wing candidate was heavily favored to win.

Lula's reelection instead renews questions about the country's fiscal outlook and the pace of future interest rate cuts.

Until Lula's government establishes a more credible fiscal framework, Brazil faces "a period of higher rates, elevated sensitivity to policy announcements, and a rate cutting cycle more likely than not to stall," Benjamin Mandel, an economist at Jubarte Capital, warned ahead of the election outcome.

Because investors have seen the election outcome as having direct bearing on Brazil's fiscal discipline, Mandel described any reaction to the election as "likely to be binary and highly persistent," in a Friday note.

articles.title: The problem with ‘woke’ businesses: Good intentions don’t pay the bills.
articles.summary: Starting a business to advance a cause is perfectly fine. But expecting that cause to keep the business alive is another matter entirely.
articles.body:
In April, Denver’s only lesbian bar closed . Its owners cited financial difficulties after a disagreement between management and employees. In 2025, a bar in Los Angeles called The Ruby Fruit also closed after a fire and alleged complaints from employees about its workplace policies. That same year, a “radically inclusive” feminist bookstore in New York closed, citing financial, health and structural difficulties, as well as “racist, classist violence from ‘neighbors.’”

Here in my hometown of Philly, we saw in 2022 the closure of progressive cafe Mina’s World, a coffee shop emphasizing social justice, and more recently Marsha’s, the city’s “first women’s sports bar.”

A 40-year-old gay bar in Salt Lake City saw its demise last year after employees tried to unionize and its owners couldn’t navigate the financial effects of continuing protests. But some good news: the Last Ditch bar in western Massachusetts, made globally famous over the summer after suffering severe backlash from its community over its mask-required policy, is still hanging on, despite facing significant financial strain and continued public backlash.

There’s a pattern here worth confronting: The failure rate of bars, for example, is already high. Unfortunately some business owners are making it even harder for themselves. They are building their identities around progressive causes and discovering that ideological solidarity doesn’t always translate into financial sustainability.

Starting a progressive — or some may say “woke” — establishment may sound like a great idea at first. But do these founders have a business education? They don’t seem to do the market research necessary to justify the investment (yes, women’s support has gained in popularity but are there enough local women’s sports fans to support a bar?). Like one of the owners of The Last Ditch, who admitted she was living out of her car, they are oftentimes under-capitalized. Do they have a financial plan?

Good intentions don’t pay rent. Solidarity doesn’t make payroll. And even the most passionate community can’t keep a business alive if customers aren’t spending enough money.

Progressive businesses seem to attract a certain kind of crowd that makes it harder for them to succeed. The crowd is younger, mobile and less reliable. Being young, they’re oftentimes more idealistic than realistic — perhaps even a little naive. The employees demand rights and guarantees that cannot be guaranteed, and seem to frequently fight the very people who employ them. Their customers come in from the fringe and spend too little money and too much time getting involved in the establishment’s mission, policies and operations instead of just enjoying the product.

According to a recent Bentley-Gallup survey , 53 percent of Americans say businesses should stay out of public debates altogether. That doesn’t mean people oppose the causes themselves. It means many consumers would rather businesses focus on what they’re supposed to be selling. People are tired of all the fighting, protesting, dissenting and arguing. They just want a beer! Is that so hard to ask?

I’m sure that not all woke businesses fail. It’s that businesses fail when their political mission becomes more important than their customers, employees, financial discipline and profitability.

Not a few blocks away from Marsha’s stands Woody’s, a popular gay bar in Philly. It’s been around for decades. I am sure that its owners support many of the causes that these other failed establishments support. But they clearly understand how to run a business.

They get that their bar needs to be inclusive of everyone, which is why many people I know, straight and gay, go there to drink and dance late night on a Saturday. They’re not asked to wear a mask, sign a petition or — good God — watch the WNBA. There’s no judgment. No politics. Just beer and music.

Starting a business to advance a cause (think Patagonia ) is perfectly fine. But expecting that cause to keep the business alive is another matter entirely.

Businesses are meant to generate profits. They need customers from all walks of life who spend their money. They need employees who won’t discriminate based on someone’s political beliefs (and they can take that money and use it to support their cause, like so many of us do). As Don Draper famously said , “that’s what the money’s for!”

Chick-fil-A has become one of America’s most successful restaurant chains despite its history of controversy over gay rights. Its executives understand something that too many politically driven entrepreneurs forget: You don’t have to agree with your customers to take their money.

You want to fight racism? Support transgender rights? Save the planet? That’s fine. Build a business that makes money, treats its employees fairly and welcomes customers who don’t necessarily share your views. Then use your profits to advance whatever cause you believe in. Because if your business fails, you’re not helping anyone. And your landlord couldn’t care less how progressive you are.

Gene Marks is founder of the Marks Group, a small-business consulting firm.

articles.summary: Meta laid out a plan to raise up to $95 billion for its AI infrastructure build-out on Monday.
articles.body:
Meta ( META ) stock slid 2% Monday morning as the company said it plans to raise up to $95 billion through equity financing with an initial $35 billion raise in common and preferred stock to fund its aggressive AI infrastructure build-out.

Its main chip suppliers, Nvidia ( NVDA ), AMD ( AMD ), and Broadcom ( AVGO ), expressed interest in purchasing up to $5 billion in aggregate of these shares, the company said.

The initial raise includes about $22.5 billion in Class A common stock and $12.5 billion in Series A mandatory convertible preferred stock.

Meta said the capital raised will support continued momentum across its "core business and emerging AI opportunities."

Those initiatives include its family of apps, AI agent Muse, and infrastructure build-out, among others.

Meta has been aggressively building out compute capacity and advancing its AI capabilities, with the recent launch of Muse, which has become a major consumer-facing hit.
