articles.title: CoreWeave, AI landlord stocks sink to lowest levels in more than a year as the price of insuring CoreWeave's debt doubles
articles.summary: Wall Street is still paying up for the companies that buy AI computing power while dumping the neoclouds that borrowed billions to rent it out.
articles.body:
Wall Street is still paying up for the companies that buy AI computing power. It's dumping the ones that borrowed billions to rent it out.

Think of the neoclouds as AI's landlords. They take on heavy debt to buy Nvidia ( NVDA ) chips, then rent out the computing power to companies building AI. That works fine while money is cheap and tenants keep signing leases. It gets dicey when lenders start asking questions.

They're asking now. A Yahoo Finance basket of eight neoclouds has lost more than 40% since late July. Microsoft ( MSFT ), one of the biggest renters of AI computing power, has gained nearly as much.

CoreWeave ( CRWV ), the biggest of the group, closed Friday at its lowest since May 2025 and is on track to do it again Monday. IREN ( IREN ), Core Scientific ( CORZ ), and Cipher Mining ( CIFR ) are at their lowest in more than a year, and Galaxy Digital ( GLXY ) hit a record low for its US listing.

The bond market is sending the same message

Investors can buy insurance against a company defaulting on its debt, called a credit default swap . For CoreWeave, that insurance now costs more than twice as much as it did in early June, according to Bloomberg data.

At today's price, the market is effectively betting on better-than-even odds that CoreWeave defaults within five years, by Yahoo Finance calculations. That's double the odds of a year ago. It's a price with plenty of fear baked in, not a forecast.

Last week, CoreWeave flirted with a bear trap — a dip that snaps back and burns traders betting on more losses. The bounce didn't stick, and the cost of insuring its debt kept climbing.

Nebius ( NBIS ) is the exception. It's at its lowest only since July and still up big this year. It carries less debt than CoreWeave, and investors are sorting the group by balance sheet.

The money hasn't dried up — it's gotten picky

Elon Musk put it bluntly Sunday on X: Lenders have "almost entirely shut off access to money" for companies that depend on AI data centers for their revenue. SpaceX ( SPCX ), with its Starlink and launch businesses behind it, just borrowed $40 billion for AI chips.

Musk isn't a neutral observer. SpaceX ( SPCX ), which absorbed his AI startup xAI in February, now rents out its own data centers to AI developers, including Anthropic and Google. Every neocloud that can't raise money is one less rival for those customers. And in a shakeout, the buyer with the strongest balance sheet usually gets the best deals.

Wall Street's big money managers see the same divergence. In a BofA Global Research survey, fund managers who buy convertible bonds (a stock-and-debt hybrid that AI companies have used to raise cash) named an AI bubble as their top near-term worry. They're crowding into the safest borrowers, even though most don't expect AI spending to slow for at least another year.

articles.body:
Anthropic's long-awaited filing on Monday offered investors a fresh glimpse into the fortunes at stake for some of the biggest names in tech and finance ahead of the artificial intelligence startup's stock market debut.

The maker of Claude is preparing for a potential November listing that could rival SpaceX's ( SPCX ) debut as the largest IPO in history.

The new filing details a financing agreement with Alphabet, Google's parent company ( GOOG , GOOGL ), that could provide Anthropic with up to $20 billion in additional funding.

The arrangement could be reduced by as much as $10 billion if Google exercises an option to purchase nonvoting Anthropic stock in a private placement alongside the IPO, at the offering price.

Anthropic publicly files IPO prospectus, noting strong revenue growth and massive spending

Anthropic's IPO filing reveals $430 billion in locked-in AI computing

Anthropic plans to go public at a time when AI tokens have never been cheaper

Google's financing agreement carries a 14.99% ownership cap, which the company can waive. No funds had been drawn under the arrangement as of June 30, according to the filing.

Amazon ( AMZN ), one of Anthropic's other biggest backers, holds approximately $6.2 billion in outstanding convertible notes that could become roughly 1.84 billion nonvoting shares when the AI startup completes its IPO, according to the filing.

The conversion is subject to a 12% ownership cap, which Amazon can waive. Any notes that cannot convert because of the restriction would remain outstanding and could convert into additional shares following the offering.

The carrying value of Amazon's various Anthropic investments totaled $190.4 billion, according to a July disclosure.

Amazon has separately agreed to provide up to $15 billion in additional financing tied to Anthropic hitting computing capacity milestones. Neither of the tech giants' facilities had been drawn as of June 30.

But Amazon and Google stand to benefit from far more than their equity investment in the startup. Anthropic is also a major customer of Amazon Web Services, which provides cloud computing capacity and distributes the company's AI models to customers.

Anthropic generated $16.3 billion in revenue during the first half of 2026, exceeding its sales for all of last year. But the company also spent nearly $9 billion on computing and infrastructure during those six months, according to the filing.

The AI developer has also committed to spending roughly $450 billion on cloud computing in the coming years, including agreements with Amazon and Google.

"Amazon is going to be the biggest beneficiary because it can win twice," Harrison Rolfes, a senior analyst with PitchBook, told Yahoo Finance last month. It wins on compute sales, it wins on investment," he added.

articles.title: 5 unexpected risk factors Anthropic is worried about
articles.summary: In its S-1 filing for IPO, Anthropic outlined many other fascinating risks besides those about to AI spending and financing and the Terminator-esque threats...
articles.body:
Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) on Monday filed paperwork for its blockbuster IPO , widely anticipated to be the largest in history, underscoring the massive expectations for the frontier AI lab and a testament to Wall Street's excitement around the AI transformation.

It'll trade on the Nasdaq under the symbol "ANT."

The documents, known as an S-1 ( read the whole thing here ), give us the clearest picture yet of Anthropic's business. The financials are fascinating — the company took in $16 billion while losing over $80 billion in the first half of the year — and the Terminator-esque warnings of AI safety are there.

But some of the juiciest parts come from the section on risk factors, which outline all the threats facing the company. But no one is more creatively pessimistic than a good securities lawyer. (One of those risks is about the effects of negative media coverage of, you guessed it, risks.)

There are plenty of obvious and boilerplate risks. But here are five unexpected risks Anthropic is worried about and that investors should keep a close eye on:

Anthropic's customer base is narrow and sensitive to downturns

"A significant portion of our customer base consists of startups and technology-oriented enterprises that may be more sensitive to adverse macroeconomic conditions and may reduce or delay spending during a downturn," the company wrote.

It's a perk of the AI business that frontier labs can count the most ambitious technology companies in the country as their customers. Who needs lots of customers when you have the best ones? That's a sweet deal in good times. But as the risk factor states, having a basket of clients so heavily concentrated in one sector can spell trouble if economic conditions change.

Anthropic publicly files IPO prospectus, noting strong revenue growth and massive spending

Anthropic's IPO filing reveals $430 billion in locked-in AI computing

Anthropic plans to go public at a time when AI tokens have never been cheaper

If that's not enough, the company notes that "A substantial portion of our revenue and accounts receivable is driven by a limited number of customers and distribution channels."

In other words, small in number and potentially high in sensitivity.

For all the talk of the tech giants struggling to meet the expectations of this AI moment, fending off nagging questions about ROI on huge AI spending, it's important to remember they were gigantic, profitable businesses before ChatGPT exploded onto the scene. They are advertising juggernauts, e-commerce meccas, and cloud service titans. Anthropic, on the other hand, doesn't have a hugely successful legacy business. There's no Facebook or Amazon Prime. It's mostly just Claude.

articles.title: Anthropic plans to go public at a time when AI tokens have never been cheaper
articles.summary: Anthropic plans to go public at a time when token prices for running AI models are at their lowest.
articles.body:
Anthropic's ( ANTH.PVT ) highly anticipated IPO comes as the cost of running AI models continues to decline, raising questions about pricing pressure amid intensifying competition.

The AI developer that makes the Claude chatbot publicly filed paperwork for an IPO on Monday.

Anthropic generates revenue primarily through usage-based pricing, metered in tokens. Customers are charged rates that vary by Claude model, as well as subscription fees for its products. The company said consumption-based revenue accounted for 80% of total revenue in the first half of 2026, and subscriptions contributed the remaining 20%.

In the risks section of its filing, the AI developer noted its future growth depends on its ability to attract new customers, retain existing customers, and expand sales.

Potential risks include "changes in customer budgets or strategic priorities regarding AI investment" and "pricing changes or perception that our pricing is not competitive."

The filing comes as the cost of completing standard AI tasks has fallen by about 47% per quarter since 2023, or roughly 13 times per year, according to the AI research institute Epoch AI.

The data measured how much it costs AI models to solve problems in areas such as math, science, and games, finding that prices have fallen faster than those of other transformative technologies, including DNA sequencing, computing, and lithium batteries.

Pricing of AI tokens has become increasingly important as enterprise customers seek to reduce costs following the unbounded spending of the brief "tokenmaxxing" era .

IBM ( IBM ) CEO Arvind Krishna has noted that enterprises are increasingly focusing on their AI costs , shifting to open-weight, less expensive models that can be run locally or on private clouds.

Anthropic publicly files IPO prospectus, noting strong revenue growth and massive spending

Anthropic's IPO filing reveals $430 billion in locked-in AI computing

How this Anthropic investor is thinking through its IPO filing

"They are also getting worried if some of the AI spending is completely out of control with no real return," said Krishna during the tech company's recent earnings call.

More companies have been turning to open-source models from US and Chinese AI developers, which are less expensive and can be run locally or on private clouds.

Anthropic and OpenAI ( OPAI.PVT ) have responded to demand for more affordable models.

Earlier this month, Anthropic unveiled the Claude Haiku 5.5 model, the latest in its Claude 5.5 family, promising improved and lower costs than its predecessor.

Anthropic said Haiku 5.5 costs an average of 75% less than Haiku 4.5. Customers will pay $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens. That's in line with rival OpenAI's ( OPAI.PVT ) smallest model, GPT-6 Luna.

articles.title: Anthropic files for IPO: Losses, dividends & risks to humanity; what investors should know
articles.summary: Anthropic’s planned stock market debut captures a central AI contradiction: surging demand and huge losses, alongside warnings that its technology could
articles.body: Anthropic’s planned stock market debut captures a central AI contradiction: surging demand and huge losses, alongside warnings that its technology could threaten humanity. The Claude maker plans to list on Nasdaq as ANT, but has yet to set the number of shares or their price range. The filing offers a closer look at what investors would be buying.Founded in 2021 by former OpenAI employees, Anthropic reported $16.3 billion in revenue in the first half of 2026 alongside a net loss of $80.7 billion. Revenue growth has been rapid, largely driven by business customers using Claude and related AI software. It expects losses to continue as it invests in computing, research, safety and expansion. Remaining competitive, it says, depends on advanced models, specialist staff and capital.The disclosures go beyond finances. They confirm there are no near-term dividends, describe a share structure that gives a founder-linked vehicle decisive voting power, and detail risks ranging from regulatory scrutiny to advanced AI moving beyond human control.Here are five key takeaways.Dividends: No payouts in sightAnthropic has never declared or paid cash dividends and does not expect to do so in the foreseeable future. It plans to retain available funds and future earnings for operations and expansion. Any dividend would be at the board’s discretion, based on its financial condition and capital needs. Its credit agreement also limits payouts, even if no money is outstanding under the facility.Voting rights: A founder-linked structureAnthropic has four authorised classes of common stock, with Class A and Class N as series of Participating Common Stock. Their voting rights differ. Class A shareholders get one vote per share on general matters. Class N generally carries no voting rights; Class T, issued to the LTBT, votes only on specified matters. Class E, intended for employees other than co-founders, also lacks general voting rights, subject to protections.Class F, to be issued to Founder LLC, carries votes equal to 50.1% of total voting power on general shareholder matters, including elections of directors other than Class T directors. Votes will be cast under the Founder LLC agreement, potentially limiting ordinary shareholders’ influence after listing.Losses: An $80.7 billion half-year hitAnthropic’s net loss rose from $1.5 billion in 2023 to $8.3 billion in 2024 and $42 billion in 2025. In the six months to 30 June 2026, it lost $80.7 billion, compared with nearly $13 billion a year earlier.The figure needs context: $72.4 billion of the first-half loss came from changes in the fair value of convertible promissory notes, derivative liabilities and SAFEs, primarily as the value of outstanding notes rose alongside Anthropic’s valuation. The net loss is not a simple measure of cash spent on operations. Even so, the company says it is highly capital-intensive, expects costs and losses to continue, and may never achieve or sustain profitability.Risks to humanity: The warning in the filingThe filing says advanced AI systems could “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity” without safeguards, oversight and security. Misuse, replication, weaponisation or substantial autonomy could heighten those dangers. Even isolated or simulated harmful behaviour, it says, could trigger public concern, regulatory scrutiny, litigation and reputational damage, regardless of actual harm.Anthropic also describes “closing the loop”: using successive models to design, train, test and optimise the next generation. But flaws or biases could spread into later systems and become harder to detect or fix. AI research could outpace the ability to evaluate and safeguard new models, a concern alongside chief executive Dario Amodei’s calls for more cautious development. The company warns that the danger could grow as AI systems automate more of the research and development process itself.What the founders get: A potentially historic paydayThe offering could sharply increase the paper wealth of Anthropic’s seven founders, including chief executive Dario Amodei and his sister, co-founder Daniela. Reports say the founders collectively hold nearly 500 million shares, but their post-IPO ownership and any planned sales are unclear.The final valuation, offer price and size of the sale remain undecided, making any windfall uncertain. But Class F stock could preserve substantial founder-linked control as public investors buy in.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Anthropic IPO reminds this former Amazon board member of Jeff Bezos's AWS bet
articles.summary: Anthropic will have to gain investor trust quickly as it spends big on its AI vision.
articles.body:
Investors will have to get comfortable with a public Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) spending billions of dollars to support its AI vision.

There is a precedent for this in tech: Amazon ( AMZN ), which moved from bookstore to cloud computing powerhouse and online shopping behemoth.

"It [Anthropic's IPO's] reminds me of a kind of a couple of things. I got to work with Jeff Bezos for a long period of time. And he always said, 'We're willing to be misunderstood for long periods of time,'" Kleiner Perkins partner and Electronic Arts co-founder Bing Gordon said on Sozzi Unleashed . Gordon was also an early board member at Amazon.

"I was in the boardroom when we kept having to approve capex for AWS, kind of no profit in the short term. A lot of capex," Gordon added. "And there was one year where we said, oh my God, it's $75 billion in capex. That would be like the top 10th country in the world … The board was freaked out early on when we weren't showing free cash flow. We were investing in the future. And it is kind of like the Anthropic story. Invest in the future. The market is usually pretty bad at figuring out the three- or four-year-out returns. And so this is the bet that the capex is going to pay off in that three- or four-year period, as it did with AWS."

Anthropic publicly files IPO prospectus, noting strong revenue growth and massive spending

Anthropic's IPO filing reveals $430 billion in locked-in AI computing

Anthropic plans to go public at a time when AI tokens have never been cheaper

Anthropic's first-half 2026 revenue surged to $16.3 billion compared to $1.1 billion a year ago, the prospectus shows.

However, the filing also discloses an $80.7 billion first-half net loss and a strong signal in aggressive AI spending in the years ahead.

Investment bankers are reportedly aiming for an astronomical listing valuation at close to $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion.

Anthropic could debut on public markets before the end of November.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has to work hard to convince investors that the spending will be worth it, much like what Bezos did.

"Jeff always asks the best questions and piercing questions. And at some point, you know, you either trust your CEO or you don't," Gordon said. "And at that point, you know, we had a discussion. He's got a principle, which is disagree and commit. But he also listens to every bit of feedback. But at the end, we believed that AWS was going to be a cash-generating machine and would continue to grow."

articles.title: SpaceX's Elon Musk reveals $40 billion in debt for AI chips, warns of neoclouds
articles.summary: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said his company closed on $40 billion in financing to pay for specialized chips used to power AI.
articles.body:
SpaceX ( SPCX ) CEO Elon Musk said his company closed on $40 billion in financing to pay for specialized chips used to power AI, but warned that access to debt is drying up for companies that solely rely on data center revenue.

"As of the past few weeks, debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn't have substantial revenue independent of AI data centers," wrote Musk on X on Sunday.

Musk went on to say that SpaceX ( SPCX ) closed $40 billion in debt for Nvidia's ( NVDA ) GPUS, or graphics processing units, used for AI, but highlighted that the space company is "investment-grade" and has Starlink & rocket launch revenue.

In a follow-up post, Musk noted this "is primarily callable debt for GPU purchases that will arrive in Q1 and Q2. Not a major factor this quarter."

Musk's comments reignited concerns about the rising cost of capital and the business models of so-called neoclouds, which rent computing power to train and run AI models.

The debt disclosure comes on the heels of SpaceX's better-than-expected quarter.

The company's AI segment brought in $7.6 billion in the third quarter, more than Starlink and the rocket business combined, and more than half of SpaceX's $14.6 billion in total revenue.

Musk also took a shot at neoclouds, companies that rent out computing power and AI chips, saying they are "going to see guppy-level death and consolidation."

"Some will make it through, but not many," said Musk.

The comments following a viral chart earlier this month highlighted neocloud provider CoreWeave's ( CRWV ) spiking bond yields, underscoring concerns about the company's debt-heavy balance sheet.

Shares of CoreWeave recovered during Monday's session after opening in red territory. The stock has tumbled more than 30% over the past month.

Ines Ferre is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance.

articles.title: Oil slips $2 a barrel but stays near six-month highs on Saudi attacks
articles.summary: By Siddharth Cavale and Seher Dareen NEW YORK, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Oil prices fell $2 a barrel on Monday amid hopes of easing hostilities between the United S...
articles.body:
NEW YORK, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Oil prices fell $2 a barrel on Monday amid hopes of easing hostilities between the United States and Iran, but persistent attacks on key producer ‌Saudi Arabia kept investors wary and prices near six-month highs.

Brent crude futures were down $2.03, or 1.7%, at $114.70 at 10:37 ‌a.m. ET (1437 GMT), while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures were down $2.60, or 2.5%, at $100.71 per barrel.

On Friday, prices settled more than $3 higher, with Brent ​finishing the week up 6% and WTI ending the week 2.3% higher.

"With the jeopardy doubled by Houthi attacks into Saudi, any Brent price dips back to the lows of last week will find grateful buyers," PVM Oil Associates analyst John Evans said.

"Corrective processes are notoriously difficult to quantify, but this one has nowhere near reached any sort of levels where bulls might abandon hope," ‌he said.

Saudi Arabia, which along with Turkey ⁠and Pakistan was set to hold talks with Iranian officials in Tehran, said it was important to open channels for negotiations.

On Sunday, Qatari mediators traveled to Tehran to try ⁠to de-escalate regional tensions in coordination with the United States, an official briefed on the situation said.

Despite the mediation talks, attacks continued over the weekend, with the Houthis saying they had struck pumping stations on Saudi Arabia's East-West crude oil pipeline and Riyadh airport. ​Saudi ​Arabia said on Sunday it had intercepted more missiles and drones.

The ​effects of the US-Israeli war with Iran that began ‌on February 28 continue to reverberate as companies adjust to the disruptions of commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb Strait caused by the conflict.

October has been the worst month for attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waterways, according to data compiled by the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, a think tank that has tracked maritime security incidents worldwide since 2017.

An oil spill from a strike-damaged tanker off the coast of the United ‌Arab Emirates has widened, satellite images showed, triggering more beach closures and ​raising environmental concerns.

Elsewhere, Russian refiners are raising diesel production in October after ​the government granted export quotas following the Kremlin's supply ​agreement with the United States, two industry people close to the matter said.

Energy ministers from ‌Saudi Arabia and Singapore said state-owned oil company Saudi ​Aramco would start storing crude oil ​in Singapore from the second half of 2027, to make Aramco's supply chain in the region more resilient.
